Hey everyone, basically my question is this:

If I'm eating at a surplus (lean bulk) and then decide that I want to try cutting fat for a couple weeks, does it take some time of eating at a deficit for the body to actually start losing fat (using stored fat as energy)?

For instance, I've read before somewhere (not sure if reputable) that you can't just be eating at a surplus and be gaining weight, then suddenly decide one day that you're going to eat under your usual caloric intake and immediately start burning fat. I've read that it takes time for the body to adjust and start using those fat reserves as energy sources.

It sounds like this makes sense, but if so I'm wondering how long that period is? IIRC, it takes about a week of eating at a defect while still being active for the body to start using fat reserves as energy, but I'd definitely like some more input here as I'm quite unsure and I'm on a bit of a time crunch right now so I'm trying to schedule my bulk/cut times pretty precisely.
How Long After Switching to a "Cut" Diet to Start Losing Fat (For the Body to Use Fat Reserves as Energy)?

There is no definitive answer here since it varies from individual to individual. To really be able to pinpoint the time it takes for you to switch to fat-burning takes experience and documentation.

Buy a bodyfat-clipper and measure each day. Once in the morning, once in the early afternoon, once before hitting the sack. Then compare the day/week averages with your expected results based on your energy intake. It will tell you if your cut is working.
If you can't be bothered with bodyfat calipers, waist measurements work pretty well for this too. [Around your bellybutton not your actual waist.]

I think it's a matter of your efficiency at it. Someone who just started dieting can probably run off glycogen stores for a few days before they ever start losing any fat. Which explains the low energy fatties complain about when they try to diet for a couple days before giving up.

But when I go hiking I skip breakfast the morning of the hike because I know I'll have more constant energy running off of bodyfat stores than running off food. And I can't be bothered carrying extra food with me anyways. So for me it's < 24 hours.

So, it depends on the person, and it's kind of a skill that needs to be developed.

Fat is always being used and replenished. It's the balance between these that cause fat gain or loss over the long term.

When you start eating below maintenance, your body will prioritize glycogen(simplified, carb storage) consumption which has no effect on the amount of fat. This chemical process creates water that you will pee (commonly called 'losing water weight'), which will account for the majority of the initial weight loss, and as glycogen stores run low you'll body will prioritize fat consumption.

I've read various approximations, and often they say 'after the first 2 weeks' but this depends on how much weight you are losing, or 'after the first 4 pounds'.

If you perform a near-perfect (because perfection is hard) lean bulk with essentially zero fat gain, I have heard of people cutting just 3 weeks; however it's unlikely that you want this, because a traditional clean bulk + cut provides much more mass/strength gain than a perfect lean bulk with no cut in the same amount of time. A perfect lean bulk can be maintained all year, but an example of the kind of person who benefits would be a model who has to maintain 8% bf for his daily job, where the importance of gaining mass pales in comparison of having a job that pays for your food.

Don't schedule your entire bulk/cut schedule in one go, as even if you do everything perfectly, due to multiple factors that you can't reliably know ahead of time, you should check if you have to adjust your diet to meet your goals every 2-3 weeks.

TL;DR: approximately after you lose the first 4 pounds.
